books.title: A Brief History of Time
books.author: Stephen Hawking
books.description: The physicist's best-selling tour of the universe, from the Big Bang to black holes.
ideas: The universe had a beginning
Observations show galaxies moving away from each other. Run the film backwards and everything converges to a hot, dense starting point: the Big Bang.
Black holes
When a massive star collapses, gravity can become so strong that not even light escapes. The boundary of no return is called the event horizon.
Hawking radiation
Hawking showed that black holes aren't entirely black: quantum effects let them slowly emit radiation and, over immense times, evaporate.
Space and time are one
Einstein's relativity joined space and time into spacetime, which mass and energy bend. Gravity is the effect of that bending.

books.title: Cosmos
books.author: Carl Sagan
books.description: A poetic journey through the history of science and our place in the universe.
ideas: We are made of star stuff
The carbon, oxygen and iron in our bodies were forged inside stars that exploded long ago. We are, quite literally, a way for the cosmos to know itself.
Science as a candle in the dark
Science is a method for not fooling ourselves: test ideas against evidence, and change your mind when the evidence demands it.
The cosmic calendar
Squeeze the universe's history into one year and all of recorded human history fits into the last few seconds of December 31st.
Eratosthenes measured the Earth
Over two thousand years ago, by comparing shadows in two Egyptian cities, Eratosthenes estimated Earth's circumference with remarkable accuracy.

books.title: The Selfish Gene
books.author: Richard Dawkins
books.description: A gene's-eye view of evolution that changed how we think about natural selection.
ideas: Genes as the unit of selection
Dawkins argues that evolution is best seen from the gene's point of view: bodies are vehicles built by genes that happened to copy themselves successfully.
Selfish genes can make kind animals
Genes that lead to helping relatives or cooperating can spread, because relatives share copies of those genes. "Selfish" genes don't mean selfish behaviour.
Memes
Dawkins coined the word meme for ideas, tunes or habits that spread from mind to mind, competing and evolving a bit like genes.
Tit for tat
In repeated games, a simple strategy of cooperating first, then copying what the other did last time, does remarkably well. Cooperation can evolve from self-interest.

books.title: The Gene
books.author: Siddhartha Mukherjee
books.description: The story of the gene, from Mendel's peas to gene editing.
ideas: Mendel's peas
A monk crossing pea plants in a monastery garden discovered that traits pass down in discrete units, which we now call genes.
DNA's double helix
DNA is two strands twisted together, with bases pairing A with T and C with G. Each strand can serve as a template to copy the other.
Genes are recipes, not destinies
Most traits come from many genes interacting with environment and chance. Having a gene variant changes probabilities, not certainties.
The power and danger of editing
Tools like CRISPR let scientists change DNA precisely. They could cure diseases, but also raise deep ethical questions about changing future generations.

books.title: Sapiens
books.author: Yuval Noah Harari
books.description: A brief history of humankind, from foragers to the scientific revolution.
ideas: The cognitive revolution
Around 70,000 years ago, humans began to speak about things that don't physically exist. Shared stories let large groups of strangers cooperate.
Shared fictions
Nations, money and companies exist because many people believe in them together. These shared myths are humanity's superpower.
The agricultural trap
Farming fed more people but often meant harder work, worse diets and more disease for individuals. Wheat, Harari jokes, domesticated humans.
Money is trust
Money works because everyone believes everyone else will accept it. It's the most universal system of mutual trust ever created.
The scientific revolution began with ignorance
Modern science started when people admitted they didn't know important things, and set out to find out.

books.title: The Structure of Scientific Revolutions
books.author: Thomas S. Kuhn
books.description: How science really changes: not steadily, but through revolutionary shifts in worldview.
ideas: Paradigms
Scientists work inside a shared framework of assumptions, methods and examples. Kuhn called it a paradigm.
Normal science
Most research is puzzle-solving within the paradigm, filling in details rather than questioning the foundations.
Anomalies pile up
Results that don't fit accumulate until the old paradigm can't absorb them, and a crisis begins.
Paradigm shifts
Eventually a new framework replaces the old one, as when Copernicus moved the Sun to the centre. Afterwards, scientists see the world differently.

books.title: Little Brother
books.author: Cory Doctorow
books.description: A teenage hacker fights back after a terror attack turns San Francisco into a surveillance state. A novel about privacy, technology and civil liberties.

free.note: Released by the author under a Creative Commons license, so the full novel is included.

ideas: Surveillance changes behaviour
In the novel, constant monitoring doesn't just catch wrongdoers; it makes ordinary people afraid to act normally. Being watched all the time shrinks everyone's freedom, guilty or not.
Security theatre versus real security
Many measures look tough but don't make anyone safer, while they inconvenience millions. The book asks readers to judge security by results, not by how dramatic it looks.
The false-positive problem
When you hunt for something very rare in a huge population, even a 99% accurate test flags mostly innocent people. Mass screening drowns investigators in false alarms.
Privacy is not about hiding wrongdoing
Everyone does private things, like using the bathroom, that aren't wrong. Privacy protects the space where people think, explore and grow without an audience.
Understand the tools to stay free
The main character survives because he understands how the technology works: encryption, networks and their weak points. Technical literacy becomes a form of civic power.

books.title: Down and Out in the Magic Kingdom
books.author: Cory Doctorow
books.description: In a post-scarcity future where death is cured and money is replaced by reputation, a man fights to keep his favourite Disney World ride from being changed.

free.note: Released by the author under a Creative Commons license, so the full novel is included.

ideas: Reputation as currency
The book imagines "Whuffie", a live score of how much others respect you, replacing money. It shows how a reputation economy could be just as unequal and anxious as a cash one.
Abundance doesn't end conflict
Even when food, health and housing are free, people still compete for attention, status and control over things they care about.
Immortality changes ambition
When backups and new bodies make death optional, characters lose urgency. The story asks whether limits are part of what gives choices meaning.
Free distribution as strategy
Doctorow released this, his first novel, free online and argued that giving it away helped it find readers and sales. Obscurity, not piracy, is the bigger threat to most creators.
